title: The form of an object is a diagram of the forces acting or that have acted on it

fields.label: Label
fields.value: The form of an object is a diagram of the forces acting or that have acted on it

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The form of any portion of matter, living or dead, can be read as a diagram of forces: from the shape of a solid one can deduce the forces that produced and maintain it, and from the shape of a fluid the forces currently acting on it, so an organism's conformation is explained by a balance of forces.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: In short, the form of an object is a “diagram of forces,” in this sense, at least, that from it we can judge of or deduce the forces that are acting or have acted upon it

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter I, “Introductory”; topic “Form as a diagram of forces”. Scope: living and non-living bodies, including whole organisms and cells

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch01-05: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.47

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Modern inverse-mechanics methods make the idea measurable in selected systems, although mapping Thompson's forces to current variables requires interpretation. Shape alone generally admits several force histories, sharply limiting discrimination and full-scope adequacy.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For structures with known material properties and boundary conditions, infer stresses or forces from shape and compare them with independently measured force fields. Accurate out-of-sample recovery would support the diagram-of-forces reading; non-unique or inaccurate recovery would limit it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Material properties and boundary conditions are usually absent.

Inverse mechanics is often non-identifiable from shape alone.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.55
analysis feasibility: 0.45
discriminating power: 0.45
data adequacy: 0.3
operationalizability: 0.55

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: For a restricted class of structures the inverse mechanical problem is a standard analysis, and public 3D and image archives supply the shapes. The claim as stated covers any portion of matter, living or dead, and shape alone does not separate force balance from a growth programme that yields the same outline. That keeps the test partial and confounded outside well-posed cases such as loaded bone or a pressurized cell.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Where material properties and loads are known, compare an observed bone, shell, or cell outline with the shape predicted by force balance. A systematic mismatch would count against reading that outline as a diagram of those forces; agreement would support the reading only for that structure.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Scans rarely include the material properties and boundary loads the deduction requires.

Many different force histories fit one preserved shape.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.4
data adequacy: 0.35
operationalizability: 0.45
analysis feasibility: 0.4
data existence: 0.6
